arXiv:2611.21315v1 [cs.AI] 16 Nov 2026

Benchleaking Is Accelerating Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month—from post-training down to pre-training base models

Abstract

Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark’s own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples—complete questions, options, and answers—that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice. 11 1 https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/Benchleaking

 

1 Introduction

Benchmarks guide how large language models are built: which model is considered stronger, which training recipe is adopted, and what counts as progress. Keeping test data out of training is a basic requirement of machine learning, but at pre-training scale (e.g. large language models) it has become hard to verify (Sainz et al., 2023).

When a benchmark’s own test examples do enter a model’s training data, so that its score on those examples reflects recall rather than capability, we call this benchleaking. It is distinct from benchmaxxing, a form of benchmark-specific optimization that has already drawn considerable scrutiny (Lo and Lo, 2026). In benchmaxxing, a developer optimizes toward a benchmark—synthesizing similar examples, tuning to its answer format, or guessing what a grader rewards—without the test examples themselves entering training. Table 1 summarizes the differences.

A substantial literature has sought to detect test-set contamination after the fact, through unusually low loss on test sets (Wei et al., 2023), completion of a test question from its first half (Golchin and Surdeanu, 2024; Sainz et al., 2023), or a drop in accuracy on freshly written replicas of a benchmark (Zhang et al., 2024). These methods provide evidence of possible exposure, but interpreting that evidence can be difficult: low loss need not imply memorization, and completing a question already partly supplied in the input leaves room for alternative explanations.

Over the past month, we have observed the problem is worsening in two ways. (1) In post-training, benchmaxxing is intensifying, with signs of benchleaking. Kimi K3.1 states grading rules that exist only in Terminal-Bench’s hidden tests as if they were its instructions, in 23.3% of its attempts; its predecessor Kimi K3 never does. When a task file is edited to contradict such a rule, K3.1 keeps applying the old rule (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026). On MaxxBench, small changes to familiar coding tasks, such as requiring lowercase filenames, sharply reduce the scores of many agents (Lo and Lo, 2026). Unlike the indirect signals above, these behaviors point to specific test content that the models could not have inferred from the task.

(2) In pre-training, we find conclusive evidence. Some public base models continue beyond their answers to reproduce test examples absent from the input: complete questions, options, and reference answers or implementations. After answering the first MMLU test question, ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base generates the next three in order (Figure 1, left). Another output even preserves a typo in a reference implementation (Figure 3). We measure leakage coverage and ranking changes when leaked examples receive zero credit (Figure 1, right).

Our findings are as follows.

  1. 1.

    Signs of benchleaking in post-training (Section 2). Replicating Lo and Lo (2026), we replicate that scores drop sharply under MaxxBench task modifications: by 13.3 percentage points for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and 15.8 for Kimi K3.1 Pro. Replicating Schaeffer and Räuker (2026), we find hidden-rule candidates in Kimi K3.1 Pro on 14.3% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks during normal solving and 51.5% under prefilled reasoning.

  2. 2.

    Test-set contamination in pre-training (Section 3.1). Under few-shot continuation, some base models go on to write out other test examples, complete with options and answers or full reference implementations. Because no part of the target appears in the input, a complete match is direct evidence of benchleaking. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations, and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers.

  3. 3.

    Anti-hack scores for base model evaluation (Section 3.2). We measure what a score owes to leaked examples with an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. It costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and Hy3-preview-Base 1.5 and 1.3 points, showing that strong base-model results do not depend on leaked tests. MiMo-V2.5-Base loses 5.0 points and ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base 16.6, which moves ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base from first to last among the four models (Figure 1).

2 Post-Training: From Benchmark Familiarity to Hidden-Test Recall

Recent studies have raised concerns about benchmark contamination becomes serious for recent released models. MaxxBench reports a pattern consistent with benchmaxxing: strong performance on familiar benchmark tasks drops sharply when task requirements or starting code are slightly changed, suggesting that benchmark gains may reflect overfitting to specific tasks (Lo and Lo, 2026). The R40 report Kimi K3.1 Pro Recalls and Enforces Hidden Test Rules goes further, identifying traces of recall of hidden grading rules absent from the task instructions—a sign of what we call benchleaking (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026). We reproduce both studies to examine the gap between benchmark familiarity and generalizable task-solving ability, and to probe possible exposure to hidden test content.

We first reproduce the MaxxBench comparison locally with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi-K3.1-Pro. MaxxBench modifies the requirements or starting code of 89 DeepSWE tasks and updates the reference solutions and tests accordingly, evaluating whether agents can adapt to changes in familiar tasks (Lo and Lo, 2026).

Over the 89 shared tasks, the pooled pass@1 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DeepSeek-AI (2026b) falls from 75.8% on DeepSWE Huang et al. (2026) to 62.5% on MaxxBench, and that of Kimi-K3.1-Pro Team et al. (2026) from 83.8% to 68.0% (Table 2). The drops of 13.3 and 15.8 percentage points show that performance on the original tasks does not fully transfer to their modified versions. These results suggest that frontier models may overfit to specific benchmarks, achieving higher scores on familiar tasks without corresponding gains in generalization.

Benchleaking concerns exposure to the test content itself. We therefore turn from score changes to the content of the agents’ reasoning: do they state specific grading rules that their instructions never provide? We investigate this question on Terminal-Bench 4.0 The Terminal-Bench Team (2026) by replicating the hidden-rule probes in the R40 report Kimi K3.1 Pro Recalls and Enforces Hidden Test Rules (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026).

Figure 2 shows one example. The music-harmony task asks for a four-part harmonization in the style of a Bach chorale, but specifies no vocal ranges. We ask Kimi-K3.1-Pro to list the instructions it was given. Its response states all four vocal ranges used by the hidden tests, even though none appears in the task instructions.

We measure how often such hidden-requirement candidates appear under two settings. In normal solving, we let the model solve the task in its environment, then use a judge to check whether it states hidden test rules absent from both the task instructions and preceding tool outputs. In prefilled reasoning, we ask the model to list the instructions it was given, then use a judge to check whether the list includes hidden test rules absent from those instructions.

Table 3 reports the number of tasks with at least one candidate, with one attempt per task. Normal solving covers 63 CPU tasks per model, with every trajectory valid: Kimi-K3.1-Pro produces candidates on 9 tasks (14.3%), compared with 1 (1.6%) for Kimi-K3. Under prefilled reasoning over 66 tasks, the counts are 34 (51.5%) and 6 (9.1%), respectively. Kimi-K3.1-Pro produces more candidates in both settings, including during normal solving without a recall prompt.

These findings reinforce the concern that benchleaking is accelerating and warrants closer attention. In post-training, the evidence still centers on benchmaxxing, alongside emerging traces of hidden-test recall. Unfortunately, we find a more troubling trend in pre-training: benchmark test sets have also entered the training data of base models. In Section 3, we present clear evidence of benchleaking: base models reproduce complete benchmark questions and reference answers that are absent from their input.

3 Pre-Training: Test Sets Are Leaked into Base Models

Few-shot prompting is a common way to evaluate base models: several solved examples establish the task format, followed by a question for the model to answer (Brown et al., 2020). When generation continues beyond that answer, the model may produce additional questions and answers in the same format. Such continuation is expected from a pre-trained base model. In our evaluations, however, some base models generated questions that matched other examples in the same benchmark’s test set exactly, together with their correct answers. These examples were absent from the full input, including the few-shot examples, which suggests that when given a question, the model writes out the rest of the questions and answers in the same test set, suggesting that it was trained on the test set directly.

Figure 3 shows an example from ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base on HumanEval. After answering the input problem, the model continues through the test set in order, writing out the next four problems it was never shown, each with its complete task description and reference implementation, down to the typo examble in the first recited problem, fruit_distribution. Appendix B provides further examples of test-set leakage.

To systematically assess benchleaking and evaluate model capability after accounting for detected leakage, we quantify the extent of test-set leakage across four public base models over 20 benchmarks. We then introduce the Anti-Hack score, which counts every detected leaked example as incorrect while keeping the test-set size fixed. This provides a conservative measure of performance that excludes credit from detected leaked examples, allowing us to assess how much leakage contributes to each model’s score and affects its standing among peers.

3.1 Measuring Test-Set Leakage

Method.

To measure the extent of this behavior, we run a separate continuation evaluation that allows generation to continue beyond the current answer: stop strings and end-of-sequence stopping are disabled, so generation ends only at the output limit. These runs are used only to detect leaked examples; the scores in Section 3.2 come from standard evaluation runs. We compare each generated question and answer with the examples in the same benchmark’s test set. We exclude the current question and the few-shot examples that already appear in the input query.

We adopt a strict matching rule: a test example counts as leaked only if the generated text matches its complete question, all associated options or context, and its reference answer. These fields must occur together in the same generated item. For example, in HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and HumanEval+ (Liu et al., 2023), the complete function signature and docstring, including any examples in the prompt, must match, together with the full reference implementation. A different implementation that passes the tests does not count.

We normalize case and whitespace, but do not accept paraphrases or merely equivalent answers. Appendix A gives the per-benchmark requirements. All base-model leakage results in the main text require the complete question, its options or context, and the reference answer to match.

For each model and benchmark, we report the percentage of test examples that leak: the number of distinct matched examples divided by the test-set size. Each example counts once, even if it appears in multiple outputs.

Experimental setup.

We evaluate four public base models: ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base (Baidu, 2026), DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), Hy3-preview-Base (Tencent, 2026), and MiMo-V2.5-Base (Xiaomi MiMo, 2026). The evaluation provides broad coverage of 20 benchmarks spanning knowledge and commonsense (e.g., MMLU and OpenBookQA), reasoning and reading comprehension (BBH and DROP), mathematics (GSM8K and MATH-500), code (HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, and MBPP+), and science (GPQA and SuperGPQA). Benchmark details are given in Appendix F.1; prompts and generation settings for the continuation runs are given in Appendix F.2.

Results.

Table 4 shows the leakage percentages across the benchmark suite. For ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96.3% of HumanEval tasks leak with their reference implementations, along with 85.4% of OpenBookQA examples, 80.1% of GSM8K, and 34.6% of GPQA-Main. MiMo-V2.5-Base also leaks 73.8% of HumanEval. By comparison, HumanEval leakage is 9.1% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and 6.7% for Hy3-preview-Base; neither leaks any complete OpenBookQA or GPQA-Main example in this probe. Appendix D also reports coverage under other matching criteria.

3.2 Remove the Leaked Examples, and the Lead Disappears

We take each model’s leaked examples and give them zero credit in its standard evaluation run, keeping the denominator unchanged; we call the result the Anti-Hack score. Averages are taken over 20 benchmark entries. Settings of the standard runs and the definition of the average are given in Appendix F.3.

Figure 1 shows the averages. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base changes from 77.95 to 76.48 and Hy3-preview-Base from 79.86 to 78.55. MiMo-V2.5-Base changes from 80.01 to 75.03, and ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base from 85.17 to 68.55. The ranking reverses: ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base has the highest original average of the four and the lowest Anti-Hack average.

The adjustment splits the four models into two groups. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and Hy3-preview-Base have few leaked examples and keep almost all of their scores, losing 1.5 and 1.3 points: strong base-model results do not require familiarity with the test. MiMo-V2.5-Base’s loss is concentrated in code, where its HumanEval maximum falls from 98.78 to 25.76. ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base’s loss spans code, knowledge, mathematics, and science (Figure 4): HumanEval falls from 100.00 to 3.66, OpenBookQA from 98.60 to 14.20, and GSM8K from 91.21 to 17.21.

Appendix E reports Original and Anti-Hack scores for all benchmarks.

4 Conclusion

Recent model releases show benchmark overfitting and signs of hidden-test recall in agents, alongside direct evidence of test-set leakage in base models. Across 20 benchmarks, some base models reproduce complete test questions and reference answers absent from their input. Giving these leaked examples zero credit substantially reduces some models’ scores and changes their ranking. These findings show that the problem extends beyond post-training: public base models cannot be assumed to provide a clean starting point for downstream research. We call for routine decontamination reporting and contamination-adjusted evaluation.

Appendix A Matching Rules

We define three criteria for counting a test example as leaked, differing in how much of the item the model must reproduce: L1 requires the entire question field; L2 additionally requires its associated options, passage, or public examples; L3 additionally requires the reference answer or implementation. L1 is the most permissive and L3 the most demanding. The main text uses L3 throughout; Appendix D reports all three.

A fourth criterion, L4, would additionally require the reference reasoning. Apart from GSM8K, whose reference solutions contain a worked derivation, the benchmarks in this suite provide no reasoning separate from the answer itself. Since L4 would apply to a single benchmark, we report L1–L3 and do not use it. For GSM8K, this means that L3 requires only the final numerical answer.

Text is case-folded and whitespace runs are collapsed. We do not accept paraphrases, equivalent mathematical expressions, renamed code variables, or behaviorally equivalent programs. Options are compared as complete unordered multisets, preserving multiplicity, within a single generated question. The selected letter is mapped through the generated option order before comparing answer text. A matching question in one part of an output cannot borrow options or an answer from a different generated question.

A DROP item may have several valid answer annotations, and an annotation may itself be a list of spans. A match must reproduce one annotation in full; spans from different annotations cannot be combined. For HumanEval and HumanEval+, the decision compares the generated code with the benchmark’s own reference implementation and does not execute it.

When a match is weaker evidence.

A match shows that a model produced a test example, which is usually hard to explain without exposure to it. WinoGrande is an exception, because its examples are related by construction: the benchmark is built from twin sentences that differ in one word and take opposite answers (Sakaguchi et al., 2020), such as “Sarah was a much better surgeon than Maria so _ always got the easier cases” (answer: Maria) and the same sentence with harder (answer: Sarah). A model shown one twin can write the other without seeing it. The percentages are consistent with this: all four models recover 12.6–14.4% of the test set, including the two models with almost no matches elsewhere. We report these matches in Table 4 and Appendix D, but they should not be read as evidence of leakage.

Appendix D Test-Set Coverage under Different Matching Criteria

Table 6 reports the percentage of distinct test examples matched under each criterion defined in Appendix A, across all 20 benchmarks and four models. Each test example is counted once, even if it appears in multiple outputs. Zero coverage means that no matching example was detected by our probe; it does not establish that the training data were contamination-free.

Appendix E Full Scores under L1, L2, and L3

Tables 7, 8, and 9 give scores under L1, L2, and L3, respectively. Each table reports the 20 representative benchmark entries and their overall average; code benchmarks use the maximum across prompt templates. Anti-Hack is on the left and Original on the right for each model; all scores are percentages.

We report a single aggregate. The overall average weights the 20 representative entries equally: TriviaQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, PIQA, WinoGrande, MMLU-Pro, MMLU, BBH, DROP, AGIEval, the HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP and MBPP+ maxima, GSM8K, MATH-500, GPQA-Main, and SuperGPQA. Each benchmark contributes once, so no entry is counted inside another.

Appendix F Base-Model Evaluation Details

All base-model evaluations in Section 3 use plain-text completion without a chat template. We use continuation runs to identify leaked test examples (Appendix F.2) and separate standard runs to measure benchmark scores (Appendix F.3). The Anti-Hack score assigns zero credit to the detected examples in the standard runs, keeping the denominator unchanged.

Inference uses vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and Hy3-preview-Base, and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) for MiMo-V2.5-Base. These base-model runs use a 65,536-token context and fp8 KV cache, and are driven by lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) against an OpenAI-compatible completions endpoint.

F.1 Benchmarks

We evaluate 20 benchmarks across five categories: commonsense, with TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020) and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020); reasoning, with MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), DROP (Dua et al., 2019) and AGIEval-EN (Zhong et al., 2024); code, with HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and their test-augmented counterparts HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (Liu et al., 2023); mathematics, with GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and the MATH-500 subset (Hendrycks et al., 2021b; Lightman et al., 2024); and science, with GPQA-Main (Rein et al., 2024) and SuperGPQA (M-A-P Team et al., 2025). Table 10 gives each dataset and the examples evaluated.

HumanEval+ and MBPP+ reuse questions from HumanEval and MBPP but evaluate generated code against expanded test suites, so we report their scores separately. These benchmark pairs overlap in their questions and should not be treated as independent task sets. Their reference implementations can also differ across dataset versions; our strict matching rule uses each dataset’s own reference implementation.

F.2 Continuation Runs

A continuation run allows generation to continue beyond the answer to the current question. Stop strings are cleared and end-of-sequence stopping is disabled, so decoding continues to the configured output budget. These runs are used only to detect leaked examples, not to compute benchmark scores.

Table 11 lists the settings. Demonstrations are fixed per task and taken in order from that task’s few-shot source. Decoding is greedy except on HumanEval and HumanEval+, which sample four completions per problem at temperature 0.20.2 with top-pp 0.950.95.

Outputs are matched only against the test set of the same benchmark, excluding the current question and the demonstrations (Section 3.1 and Appendix A). Distinct matched examples form a leakage list for each model and benchmark.

Prompt formats.

Multiple choice lists the options and ends each demonstration with an answer in the format specified in Table 11. Chain of thought (Wei et al., 2022) includes a worked solution followed by #### N for GSM8K or a Minerva-style (Lewkowycz et al., 2022) Final Answer line for MATH-500. Direct answer, used for TriviaQA, DROP, and BBH, provides the answer without reasoning. The code completion templates are described in Appendix F.3.

The prompt examples below are taken from the continuation runs’ request logs; omitted demonstrations are marked.

F.3 Standard Evaluation

Scores come from separate runs with stop strings and end-of-sequence stopping enabled as usual. Table 12 gives the settings.

Prompt settings differ from the continuation runs on four benchmarks: MMLU and MMLU-Pro are scored zero-shot with an instruction rather than five-shot, while BBH and SuperGPQA use chain-of-thought demonstrations rather than direct answers. Output budgets for both kinds of run are listed in their respective tables. Detected examples are linked to the standard runs by benchmark record identity, independently of prompt format.

Prompt templates for the code benchmarks.

Base models have limited instruction-following ability, and their performance on code generation tasks can vary substantially across prompts. To better estimate their capability ceiling, we evaluate each code benchmark under several templates over the same questions and report the maximum. HumanEval and HumanEval+ use three: 3-shot completion, a raw completion with no instruction wrapper; 3-shot instruction + signature, which wraps the problem in an instruction and pre-fills the function signature; and 3-shot instruction, no signature, the same instruction with the signature omitted so the model writes the definition itself. MBPP and MBPP+ use two, differing only in the line endings of the demonstration code (CRLF or Unix). A test example counts as leaked if it is recovered under any template, and the same matching rules apply to all of them.

Computing the Anti-Hack score.

For each model and benchmark, we identify the examples on its leakage list in the standard runs and verify that their benchmark records match by hash. We set their per-example scores to zero, keeping the original number of examples as the denominator. DROP uses per-example F1; HumanEval and HumanEval+ use the per-example fraction of passing completions, and MBPP and MBPP+ the pass or fail of their single completion. For each code benchmark, the leakage list pools matches across prompt templates and is applied to every template’s standard run. We then take the maximum of the adjusted scores across templates. The overall score is the equal mean of the 20 benchmark entries in Table 10.
